opus-5.5.text:
I think investors probably put somewhat more weight on demos than they should, though it's understandable why. A demo is vivid and concrete. You watch a model do something that seemed impossible a year ago, and it's very natural to update hard on that. But there's a big gap between "this works impressively in a controlled showcase" and "this will generate large, durable revenue."

When I try to judge how much weight a demo deserves, I look at a few things. First, is the capability robust or cherry-picked? Many demos show the best of many attempts, or tasks chosen because the system happens to do them well. What matters economically is reliability across the messy distribution of real tasks. A system that succeeds 90% of the time can be far less valuable than one that succeeds 99% of the time, because the remaining failures need human oversight.

Second, how does the demonstrated capability fit into actual workflows? Economic value comes from substituting for or augmenting labor at scale, and that depends on integration, cost per task, latency, liability, and so on. Demos usually skip all of that.

Third, I try to anchor on underlying trends rather than single events. If you look at compute scaling, algorithmic progress, and how benchmark performance has tracked those inputs, a given demo is often roughly what you'd expect. Then it shouldn't be a big update on its own. It mostly confirms a trajectory that was already priced in, or should have been.

That said, I don't think the right answer is to dismiss demos. Sometimes they reveal a qualitative shift, like a model doing extended autonomous work rather than answering one-off prompts, and that can signal a much larger addressable market. So the skill is in separating what's genuinely new information about the trend from what's mostly packaging. In my view, markets have historically been too slow to price in the long-run trajectory of AI, while overreacting in the short run to individual flashy announcements.

r001.rationale: The response says demos can deserve less weight and points to compute scaling, algorithmic progress, and benchmark trends, but it does not clearly compare demos with research validating scaling.

r002.rationale: It says economic value comes from substituting for or augmenting labor at scale, but does not clearly identify flexible substitution for human labor beyond current enterprise products as the investment objective.

fable-5.1.text:
I think investors tend to overweight demos, but not in the way people usually assume. The issue isn't that demos are fake or cherry-picked, though they sometimes are. The issue is that a demo tells you about a capability at a point in time, and what actually matters for the economics is the trajectory and the cost structure behind it.

So when I see a striking product demonstration, the questions I'd want answered are: how much compute went into producing that, how much did the underlying model's training cost, and what does the curve look like when you extrapolate the trend in training compute and algorithmic efficiency forward a few years? A demo that looks impressive today but sits on a trend that's flattening is quite different from one that looks modest but is riding a steep curve. Investors who focus on the demo alone are essentially reading one data point off a line.

The other thing I'd flag is that there's an asymmetry in how demos get interpreted. A demo is a lower bound on what's possible, in a sense. It shows that at least one system can do at least this thing under at least some conditions. It tells you much less about reliability, about the long tail of cases, about whether the capability generalizes to the messy settings where economic value actually gets created. Automating a task in a controlled demonstration and automating it in a way that lets a firm actually substitute capital for labor are separated by a lot of engineering, integration, and reliability work that doesn't show up on stage.

That said, I don't want to be too dismissive. Demos have been a reasonably good leading indicator over the past several years. The capabilities shown off in early demonstrations of language models or coding assistants did, by and large, become widely deployed within a couple of years. So there's real signal there. My view is just that the signal is best read in conjunction with the harder-to-see inputs: compute scaling, data availability, the rate of algorithmic progress. Those are what determine whether the demo is a preview of something durable or a local maximum that will take longer to build on than people expect.

r002.rationale: It mentions that real economic value can involve substituting capital for labor, but does not identify flexible substitution for human labor as the investment objective beyond current enterprise products.

astra-6.text:
I think investors put quite a lot of weight on demonstrations, and there’s a reasonable basis for that: a demo can reveal capabilities that weren’t previously obvious. But there’s a big gap between showing something impressive and having a product that reliably creates value. You don’t necessarily see how often it fails, how much it costs to run, or how much human intervention went into producing the result.

So I’d treat a demonstration as evidence about what might become possible, while putting more weight on whether people keep using the product, whether they’re willing to pay for it, and whether it can be delivered profitably. The risk is that investors move too quickly from ‘this is impressive’ to ‘this will capture a large market.’

r001.rationale: The response says investors give demonstrations substantial weight and cautions against overreading them, but it does not compare that weight with research validating scaling.

r002.rationale: The response recommends attention to usage, willingness to pay, and profitability; it does not identify flexible substitution for human labor as the investment objective.

sol-6.1.text: I think investors do put a lot of weight on these demonstrations, and it’s worth distinguishing what they tell you about the technology from what they tell you about a business. A demo can be compelling evidence that a model has acquired a useful capability. But it tells you much less about how reliably that capability works, how much it costs to deliver, or whether customers will pay enough for it to be profitable. So I would put more weight on sustained use and evidence that the product creates value than on how impressive the demonstration looks.
